I have experienced many films this year that have greatly enriched my life for having witnessed them; Mizoguchi, Bergman, Bertolucci, Teshigahara and Tarkovsky have all touched me more than most film-makers with masterfully significant works, but one auteur in particular has staked his flag at the pinnacle. After the delirious master-class of Harakiri, the elegance of Samurai Rebellion and startling Kwaidan, Masaki Kobayashi has crushed my soul and moved me to tears with his greatest achievement - 'The Human Condition', and while I am only one third through a 10 hour epic journey, I am already willing to claim this as the greatest film I have ever seen.

This review may contain spoilers. I can handle the truth.

'I'm boarding this run-down truck, but you're trying to catch the train of humanism before it's too late. You seem willing to pay the fare, no matter how high.'

I'll never not be fascinated by the Japanese, their open-mindedness to cross-examine themselves as a nation and their selfless willingness to paint themselves in a less favorable light in movies. It is an act of infinite humility that elicits the most noble of reactions from me – my utmost respect.

Review by {Todd} 2

"Freedom? You must be a poet." - Prison Guard,

Wow....

I honestly don't believe that I can do this film justice with a review so I'll simply say it's a really interesting and powerful script that's backed up by great performances and Masaki Kobayashi's masterwork. I'm so glad I finally watched this. The film lived up to all of my expectations and overwhelmed me a bit. I was intimidated by the length of The Human Condition I but honestly the pacing is really great and the story is so engaging that it didn't bother me at all. Also the themes of socialism, pacifism, and anti-colonialism are right up my alley.

It's phenomenal.

Review by Robert Beksinski 11

The Human Condition is a 9 and a half hour long film journey, that I personally hail as the greatest film ever made.

I'm not even sure where to begin. As the title suggests, the film has an underlying psychology about the human condition. Accompanied with some of the best acting put on screen by Tatsuya Nakadai, he was able to fully express and show this development of the human psyche, while experiencing some of the harshest treatment and hardships a man can face. This will be the third time I watched this grandiose film experience, and every time it still breaks my heart by the end of the movie. It's an emotional odyssey, with its message rising above any…

Review by Dirk Diggler 4

Arguably the greatest trilogy ever made, The Human Condition is ambitious and epic in scope, but remains intimate, beautiful, emotionally affecting, contemplative and engaging all at once, as it delves on what it means to be human, on morality, compassion, decency, and human dignity or the lack thereof amidst the horrors of war. The hours flies by (it's true!) as it manages to be not only entertaining and riveting throughout its grueling length, but also deliver 10 hours of exquisite filmmaking and artistry from the beginning to the very end. That is simply a remarkable achievement. It is magnificently shot with subtle, yet dynamic camerawork and strikingly well-composed widescreen images. Review by Joshua Dysart 3

“Force has meaning only when overcoming tyranny.”

In form this is as sweeping and anti-nuanced as any text over subtext Hollywood epic, a kind of “Gone With The Wind” in its use of large vista imagery, swooning emotional romantics, and sometimes torturously on-the-nose dialogue - that also, just as often, arrives at profoundly impactful declaratives regarding the flaws of humanity.

“What is a man? Not poetry or morality. He’s a mass of lust and greed that absorbs and excretes.”

Amazing.
